lesson:
Replace `waitForLoadState('networkidle')` with explicit element visibility assertions when persistent background polling prevents the network from becoming idle, causing test timeouts despite successful page rendering.
When Playwright tests time out on `networkidle` waits because shared UI components like chat widgets maintain continuous server connections.
The order-history test timed out on CI at `page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')` even though the page had fully rendered. The support chat widget polls its server every 20 seconds, preventing the network from being idle for the required 500 ms window and causing the wait to hit the 30-second timeout.

Replacing the wait with `await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order history' })).toBeVisible()` reduced execution time to about two seconds. Since the chat widget is part of the shared page layout, this issue affects all pages using that layout.

lesson:
GitHub CLI list commands silently truncate results at 30 items unless an explicit limit is provided, causing undercounting in audits.
When using `gh issue list` or `gh pr list` to count or process repository items where the total may exceed 30.
The default output of `gh issue list` and `gh pr list` is capped at 30 results without warning. To ensure complete data retrieval, always pass an explicit `--limit` (e.g., `--limit 200`). lesson:
Convert PDFs to CMYK using Ghostscript after generation because Chromium renders CSS hex colors like #000 as RGB black, which causes print vendor preflight checks to fail even when images are already in CMYK.
When a print vendor rejects a generated PDF for containing RGB content despite all embedded images being converted to CMYK.
Chromium writes CSS hex color values (e.g., `#000`) into the resulting PDF as RGB black, even if other assets are in CMYK. Changing the CSS value to `rgb(0 0 0)` does not resolve this because it is still interpreted as an RGB channel.

To fix preflight rejections caused by text color:
1. Generate the PDF normally.
2. Post-process the file with Ghostscript using `-sColorConversionStrategy=CMYK`.
3. Re-run the vendor's preflight check, which should then pass.

lesson:
LiteLLM proxy applies `rpm_limit` to the virtual key as a whole, so multiple models sharing one key share a single rate limit budget rather than having per-model allocations.
When configuring LiteLLM virtual keys for workloads that call multiple different models and encounter unexpected 429 errors despite sufficient upstream provider limits.
LiteLLM proxy applies `rpm_limit` to the virtual key as a whole, not to each model individually. If a batch job uses a single key for multiple services (e.g., a summarizer and a classifier), they share one rate limit budget. To prevent 429 errors when total requests exceed this shared limit, assign separate virtual keys with appropriate `rpm_limit` values to each service or model group.

lesson:
Service accounts require explicit membership on Google Shared Drives and the `supportsAllDrives=true` parameter to avoid 404 errors, as folder-level sharing is insufficient for Drive API access.
When a service account receives 404 File not found errors while accessing files in a Google Shared Drive despite having folder permissions.
Sharing individual folders with a service account does not grant it access to the shared drive via the Drive API. To resolve `404 File not found` errors, add the service account as a Viewer member of the shared drive itself and ensure all Drive API calls include `supportsAllDrives=true`. No changes to OAuth scopes or keys are required.

lesson:
Unescaped `#` characters in Matrix room aliases within Apprise URLs are treated as URL fragments and dropped, causing silent notification failures; percent-encode the hash as `%23` to preserve the room identifier.
When configuring Apprise notifications for Matrix rooms where the alias contains a colon or special characters that might be misinterpreted by URL parsers.
The `#` character in a URL marks the start of a fragment, which is ignored by most HTTP clients. In Apprise configurations using `matrixs://` schemes, an unescaped room alias like `#ops-alerts:example.org` causes the client to address no room at all without raising an error.

To fix this, percent-encode the hash symbol as `%23`. For example, use `matrixs://matrix.example.org/%23ops-alerts:example.org` instead of leaving it raw. Note that `notify.sh --dry-run` may not catch this issue because it resolves configuration without sending; verify fixes by sending a real test message to the target room.

lesson:
Search for name-pattern prefixes and verify configuration files before deleting functions that are referenced dynamically at runtime.
When planning to remove a function whose name follows a naming convention used by dynamic dispatch or lookup mechanisms.
A repository search for the full function name missed references because the system built handler names dynamically from configuration (e.g., `handlers[f"export_{fmt}"]`). Production configs still contained the legacy format, causing a `KeyError` after removal. Tests failed to catch this because they only exercised specific formats (`csv`, `json`) rather than the dynamic lookup path.

To safely remove such functions:
1. Search for the pattern's prefix (e.g., `export_`) in code and configuration files.
2. Verify that no active configuration entries reference the removed name.
3. Ensure tests cover the dynamic dispatch path, not just static examples.

lesson:
Lightweight git tags are not pushed by `git push --follow-tags`, causing release workflows to fail silently; always create annotated tags using `git tag -a` to ensure they are pushed and trigger CI jobs.
When creating a new version tag for a software release that relies on GitHub Actions or other CI/CD pipelines triggered by tag pushes.
The 2.4.0 release failed because the lightweight tag created with `git tag v2.4.0` was not pushed to the remote. The command `git push origin main --follow-tags` only pushes annotated tags, leaving the lightweight tag local and preventing the release job from triggering.

To fix this, recreate the tag as an annotated tag using:
```bash
git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release v2.4.0"
git push origin v2.4.0
```

Always use `git tag -a` when creating release tags to ensure they are pushed and trigger the expected workflows.

lesson:
Preflight acceptance does not guarantee compliance with stated template specifications, so unconfirmed bleed or margin discrepancies must be explicitly verified with the print vendor before final submission.
When a print file passes automated preflight checks but deviates from the vendor's documented template requirements for bleed, margins, or trim size.
The Tallowmere campaign book PDF passed preflight at 0.125 inch bleed despite the template specifying 0.25 inch. The discrepancy was never confirmed with the vendor, leaving it unclear whether the check enforces a minimum threshold or if the template documentation is outdated. Previous books used 0.25 inch, highlighting the inconsistency. Always explicitly confirm any deviation between preflight results and stated template requirements with the vendor before accepting the file for production.

lesson:
Record the exact Paged.js version and rendering path before diagnosing layout issues because v0.4.3 lacks `avoid-page` support and requires explicit handler registration for custom break attributes to function.
When debugging unexpected page breaks, missing avoid rules, or shifted spreads in a Paged.js book build where CSS properties appear ignored or elements split incorrectly.
Before diagnosing layout problems in Paged.js, record the exact version and rendering path. Version 0.4.3 supports `break-inside: avoid` but not `avoid-page`, so oversized elements must still be allowed to split. A `data-break-inside` attribute has no effect unless the pipeline registers a handler for it. Always check left and right page placement in the rendered output, because front matter and blank pages shift the spread; a class name alone proves nothing.
